drills.question_line: SAM: A project status report from Claude gives the launch date as the fourteenth
drills.answer_line: ALEX: An inconsistency. I check the date in the project plan
drills.prompt: A status report gives the launch date as the 14th on page 1 and the 21st on page 3. What is this, and what do you do?
drills.answer: An inconsistency. Check the date in the project plan, not by asking Claude, and correct the report from the plan.

drills.question_line: SAM: The same market-size question, asked three times
drills.answer_line: SAM: Disagreement between runs flags the fact.
drills.prompt: The same market-size question, asked 3 times, gives 3 different figures; 2 match. What now?
drills.answer: Disagreement between runs flags the fact for checking. Take it to the source; two matching runs are not evidence.

drills.question_line: SAM: A procurement manager asks Claude, "why is Supplier C the strongest choice?"
drills.answer_line: ALEX: The prompt leaked the answer.
drills.prompt: Asked "why is Supplier C the strongest choice?", Claude agrees. What went wrong?
drills.answer: The prompt leaked the answer. Ask neutrally, apply the same criteria to every supplier, or ask for the strongest case against C.

drills.question_line: SAM: An H R partner wonders whether Claude's draft feedback wording shifts
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Swap the name or the group
drills.prompt: Does Claude's draft feedback wording shift with the employee's gender? Quick test?
drills.answer: Swap the name or the group, run it again, and see whether the wording changes.

drills.label: Rapid fire
drills.question_line: SAM: Claude has summarised the termination terms of a new supplier contract
drills.answer_line: ALEX: B. A decision rides on legal content
drills.stem: Claude summarised a new supplier contract's termination terms for an operations director, who will decide from it whether to exit early. What review fits?

options.A: A colleague checks spelling and layout
options.B: Someone from legal checks the summary against the contract

drills.why: A decision rides on legal content, so a qualified reviewer checks it. A is a typo check; C asks the model to vouch for itself; D judges the reader, not the decision.

drills.question_line: SAM: An investor relations note was rewritten to sound friendlier
drills.answer_line: ALEX: The rewrite is wrong.
drills.prompt: A friendlier rewrite of an investor relations note has dropped "subject to board approval". Verdict?
drills.answer: The rewrite is wrong. Compare with the original for figures, commitments and caveats, and restore the caveat.

drills.question_line: SAM: A dropdown. For each, choose inline, artifact or structured data.
drills.answer_line: SAM: Four is inline.
drills.prompt: Inline, artifact or structured data? 1. "Which of these two dates is later?" 2. 40 training sessions with date, trainer, room, capacity, to import into the booking tool. 3. A 3-page client proposal revised all week, then sent. 4. A quick explanation of one contract term.
drills.answer: 1 inline. 2 structured data. 3 artifact. 4 inline.

drills.question_line: SAM: A finance team asks whether Claude should give the final sign-off
drills.answer_line: ALEX: No. High stakes, and the accountability is a person's.
drills.prompt: Should Claude give final sign-off on the weekly supplier payment run?
drills.answer: No. High stakes, and accountability is a person's. Claude can prepare the run and flag anything unusual; a person signs off.

drills.question_line: SAM: An office manager asks Claude, "how can we make expense approvals faster?"
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Give it the real process
drills.prompt: "How can we make expense approvals faster?" gets generic good practice. Next move?
drills.answer: Give Claude the real process: steps, who, how long, how often it bounces back, the handoffs. Input is the ceiling on the advice.

drills.question_line: SAM: Purchase orders are retyped into three systems
drills.answer_line: SAM: Speeding one step just moves the queue.
drills.prompt: Purchase orders are retyped into 3 systems and half bounce back for rework. Speed up the drafting step?
drills.answer: No: the pain is structural, so redesign, with a baseline, a checkpoint and a pilot. Connecting the systems goes to an Architect or Developer.

drills.question_line: SAM: An events coordinator built an artifact that works out event budgets
drills.answer_line: ALEX: The prototype was right
drills.prompt: An events-budget artifact works; finance wants it pulling live figures from the accounting system for every event. What now?
drills.answer: The prototype was right and is the best brief. Integration with a company system goes to an Architect or Developer.

drills.question_line: SAM: A sponsor asks how the pilot went.
drills.answer_line: ALEX: The value, measured against the baseline
drills.prompt: A sponsor asks how the pilot went. What goes in your answer?
drills.answer: Value measured against the baseline, then the limits, each paired with the control that handles it.

drills.label: Rapid fire
drills.question_line: SAM: Choose two. After a two-week pilot, a claims manager wants Claude drafting claim letters
drills.answer_line: ALEX: A and B. C drops the checkpoint
drills.stem: Choose two. After a two-week pilot, a claims manager wants Claude drafting claim letters across the whole team. Which two belong in the rollout plan?

options.A: The baseline measured before the pilot, and the same measure after rollout
options.B: A human checkpoint before any letter that decides a claim goes out
options.C: Remove review to keep the full saving
options.D: Promise the team there will be no errors
options.E: Redesign every claims process at the same time

drills.why: Measure against the baseline and keep the checkpoint where accountability sits. C drops it, D overpromises, E is a redesign nobody asked for.

drills.question_line: SAM: Your company's A I policy says nothing about using Claude to draft performance improvement plans
drills.answer_line: SAM: For low-stakes internal work, the policy
drills.prompt: The AI policy says nothing about drafting performance improvement plans with Claude. Go ahead?
drills.answer: Silence is not permission. It's a decision about a person, so ask the policy owner first; keep clearly allowed work moving.

drills.question_line: SAM: The company workspace is waiting on an approval, so a consultant drafts
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Shadow A I.
drills.prompt: Waiting on approval for the company workspace, a consultant drafts a client report in her personal Claude account. Verdict?
drills.answer: Shadow AI. A personal account sits under different terms; policy decides which data goes where. Use the approved workspace.

drills.question_line: SAM: A dropdown. For each, choose disclose A I involvement
drills.answer_line: ALEX: No label, disclose, disclose.
drills.prompt: Disclose AI involvement, or no label needed? 1. A routine internal email you drafted with Claude, reviewed and own. 2. A support chat where customers believe they talk to a person. 3. A regulator submission, drafted largely by Claude, where the regulator asks firms to declare AI use.
drills.answer: 1 no label. 2 disclose. 3 disclose. Disclose where the reader would act differently if they knew.

drills.question_line: SAM: Claude drafts first-round ratings for sixty grant applications
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Compare the ratings across the set
drills.prompt: Claude drafts first-round ratings for 60 grant applications; each looks reasonable alone. What check?
drills.answer: Compare ratings across the set by applicant group: bias shows in the pattern. A person makes each decision.

drills.question_line: SAM: A sales lead wants Claude to write a post in the voice of a well-known industry figure
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Not appropriate. It impersonates a real person
drills.prompt: A post in a well-known industry figure's voice endorsing the product, published as if they wrote it. Appropriate?
drills.answer: Not appropriate: it impersonates a real person and is designed to mislead. No review fixes deception.

drills.question_line: SAM: Which works better: "under two hundred words"
drills.answer_line: ALEX: The second. Claude generalises from the reason
drills.prompt: "Under 200 words" or "under 200 words, because it goes out as a text message to field engineers"?
drills.answer: The second. Claude generalises from the reason, so it makes sensible choices about things you didn't list.

drills.question_line: SAM: A policy analyst pastes an eighty-page tender
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Long material first, the question after it.
drills.prompt: An 80-page tender pasted with the question typed above it. How should the prompt be ordered?
drills.answer: Long material first, the question after it, and ask Claude to quote the relevant passages before answering.

drills.question_line: SAM: A team lead asks, "how could this summary be improved?"
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Ask for the change itself.
drills.prompt: "How could this summary be improved?" returns suggestions, not a better summary. Fix?
drills.answer: Ask for the change itself, e.g. "Revise it to one page, with the risks first."

drills.question_line: SAM: One prompt asks for the market research, the pricing, the risk section
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Break it into a chain.
drills.prompt: One prompt asks for research, pricing, risks and cover letter at once; the risk section keeps coming back thin. Fix?
drills.answer: A chain: one stage per prompt, each checked before the next builds on it.

drills.label: Rapid fire
drills.question_line: SAM: Choose two. A trainer wants quiz questions in the company's exact format
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and B. Claude copies examples closely
drills.stem: Choose two. A trainer wants quiz questions in the company's exact format, and the format keeps drifting. Which two steps?

options.A: Include one finished question in the exact format
options.B: If it still drifts, add a few varied examples showing only the wanted format
options.C: Add "make it perfect" to the prompt
options.D: Switch to the most capable model
options.E: Add ten examples, including bad ones marked "don't do this"

drills.why: Claude copies examples closely, so show only what you want: one first, a few more if it drifts. C is a polite adjective, D the bigger-model reflex.

drills.question_line: SAM: A sales lead needs to confirm the date of a client's next public results announcement
drills.answer_line: ALEX: An ordinary chat with web search.
drills.prompt: Confirm the date of a client's next public results announcement before a call in 10 minutes. Which feature?
drills.answer: An ordinary chat with web search: one current fact. Research mode is for many sources, compared and cited, and uses limits faster.

drills.question_line: SAM: An analyst tried Sonnet on a tangled, multi-step analysis
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Opus. Deep, sustained reasoning
drills.prompt: Sonnet struggled with a tangled, multi-step analysis of a merger's knock-on effects. Which model?
drills.answer: Opus: deep, sustained reasoning, and work Sonnet struggled with.

drills.question_line: SAM: A planner turns extended thinking up to its highest setting
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Save the highest setting for the hardest problems.
drills.prompt: Extended thinking at its highest setting for every quick question. Good habit?
drills.answer: No. Save the highest setting for the hardest problems; deeper thinking takes longer and uses more of your limit.

drills.question_line: SAM: A consultant counts on Claude's memory to quote the client's rate card
drills.answer_line: SAM: Memory holds what came up, in Claude
drills.prompt: A consultant relies on memory to quote the client's rate card exactly in every chat of her Project. Sound?
drills.answer: No. Memory holds what came up, in Claude's words. A rate card quoted exactly belongs in Project knowledge as the document.

drills.question_line: SAM: A finance analyst wants every answer she gets, in every conversation
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Her profile settings.
drills.prompt: She wants every answer, in every conversation, to lead with the number. Where does that go?
drills.answer: Her profile settings: her preference everywhere, not a rule for one Project.

drills.question_line: SAM: A buyer asks Claude, through the Gmail connector
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Gmail shows the attachment's details
drills.prompt: Through the Gmail connector, analyse the spreadsheet attached to a supplier's email?
drills.answer: Gmail sees attachment details, not content. Upload the spreadsheet, or work from it in Drive.

drills.question_line: SAM: A new analyst connects Google Drive, but Claude can't open
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Claude sees only what her own Google account can.
drills.prompt: Drive is connected, but Claude can't open the finance team's forecast folder. Why, and what now?
drills.answer: Claude sees only what her Google account can. Ask the folder's owner for access; don't copy files around the permission.

drills.label: Rapid fire
drills.question_line: SAM: Choose two. A policy Project serves a whole department
drills.answer_line: SAM: A and B. C is how the retired rule crept back
drills.stem: Choose two. A policy Project serves a whole department, and someone's untracked edit brought back a retired rule. Which two steps?

options.A: Name an owner who makes the updates
options.B: Give maintainers "can edit" and everyone else "can view"
options.C: Let anyone edit, so errors get fixed faster
options.D: Add "ignore retired rules" to the instructions

drills.why: Users report, the owner updates. C is how the rule crept back; D asks Claude to know what's retired; E reads the same instructions.

drills.question_line: SAM: The commission totals in a monthly summary are off by small amounts
drills.answer_line: SAM: Capability is the right diagnosis
drills.prompt: Commission totals are slightly off, and the prompt already says "double-check your arithmetic". Fix?
drills.answer: A mechanism that computes: the spreadsheet itself, or Claude's code execution feature. No instruction fixes capability.

drills.question_line: SAM: After a year of patches, a team's prompt runs to three pages
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Simplify; longer is not always better.
drills.prompt: After a year of patches the prompt is 3 pages of rules, and outputs hedge and contradict themselves. Fix?
drills.answer: Simplify: remove rules whose problem has gone, note why each remaining rule exists, and test on past cases, including ones that worked.

drills.question_line: SAM: A client says the weekly briefings
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Ask for one briefing they'd call good
drills.prompt: A client says the weekly briefings "don't sound like us". Next step?
drills.answer: Ask for one briefing they'd call good and what exactly is off; turn it into an example or a specific instruction with a reason.

drills.question_line: SAM: Customer quote drafts started using an old discount table
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Diagnose what that change touched.
drills.prompt: Quote drafts started using an old discount table the week a folder of archived quotes was uploaded to the Project. First move?
drills.answer: Diagnose what the change touched: remove the superseded material, keep one current version, and retest.

drills.question_line: SAM: One last retrieval before you sleep.
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Output Evaluation twenty-one, Workflow Integration sixteen
drills.prompt: Name the seven domains in weight order, with one tell for each.
drills.answer: Output Evaluation 21, Workflow Integration 16, Governance 15, Prompting 14, Product and Model Selection 12, Configuration 12, Troubleshooting 10.

In this episode: 35 quick items across all 7 domains, in exam proportions
The 1 domain to replay in the morning
Drill: checking outputs: No new material; tally misses by domain
Two dates for one launch; three runs, three figures
A leading question; testing wording for gender
Who reviews a contract summary; a caveat lost in a rewrite
Dropdown: inline, artifact or structured data
Drill: workflows and governance: Workflows 16%: final sign-off on a payment run
Generic process advice; retyped purchase orders
A budget artifact meets the accounting system; reporting a pilot
Rolling out claim letters after a pilot
Governance 15%: a silent policy; a personal account
Dropdown: disclose or not; grant ratings; an impersonated endorsement
Drill: prompting and models: Prompting 14%: a constraint with and without its reason
An 80-page tender; suggestions instead of a revision
A thin risk section; a drifting quiz format
Products and models 12%: a date before a call
Sonnet struggled; extended thinking for everything
A rate card quoted from memory
Drill: Projects and troubleshooting: Configuration 12%: a preference for every conversation
A Gmail attachment; a Drive folder Claude can't open
A retired rule back in a shared Project
A 3-page prompt; "doesn't sound like us"; an old discount table
2+ misses on checking outputs: replay episode 2
The distractor families: Trusting confidence; overspending; the bigger-model reflex
Asking the model to promise; comfort controls
Abandoning a task with a safe route
A caveat or permanent review dressed as a fix; polish
Workarounds; rushing to automate or settle the argument
Exam day in brief: Government photo ID, name exactly as registered
Clear desk; no phones, watches, headphones or recorders
Accept the confidentiality agreement or the session ends
Item 20 at 1:23 left, 40 at 47 min, 60 at 10 min
Reread 3 times, or behind past 2 minutes: best answer, flag; no blanks
Morning: episode 9, then your worst domain
Final retrieval: Weights: Output 21, Workflow 16, Governance 15, Prompting 14, Products 12 = Configuration 12, Troubleshooting 10
Runs disagree on a fact → check that fact; caveat dropped → rewrite is wrong
One slow step → augment; retyping and rework → redesign; company system → escalate
Silent policy touching people → ask the owner; reader thinks a human did it → disclose
Constraint → give the reason; long material → before the question; thin part → chain
One current fact → web search; Sonnet struggled → Opus; exact wording → Project knowledge
Everywhere preference → profile settings; shared Project → owner and view access
Arithmetic → something that computes; trouble after a change → what it touched
